Re: Comments on Reproductive Health Services (RIN 2900-AS31) 
Dear Secretary Collins and Acting Under Secretary Lieberman:  
The Government of Guam submits this testimony in strong objection to the U.S. Department of Veterans 
Affairs (VA) proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31, which revokes the already-limited existing access to 
abortion care and counseling for veterans and their beneficiaries through the VA medical benefits 
package and the Civilian Health and Medical Program (CHAMPVA).  
Current VA rules limit abortion access to situations of rape, incest and where the life or health of the 
pregnant patient is at risk, and also allow for abortion counseling. The RIN 2900-AS31 
proposed rule threatens the health and wellbeing of those who served our country by further limiting 
access only to cases where the patient’s life is threatened and eliminating access to counseling entirely. 
The U.S. territory of Guam is often referred to in U.S. Department of Defense circles as “the tip of the 
spear.” Guam houses Andersen Air Force Base, Marine Corps Base Camp Blaz, U.S. Naval Station 
Guam, and US Coast Guard Forces Micronesia Sector Guam. Currently, Guam is home to nearly 8,000 
active duty military personnel and approximately 23,500 U.S. military veterans. Guam consistently has 
among the highest military enlistment rates per capita in the entire United States of America.  
Of important note is the fact that sexual assault within the U.S. military is such an issue that the 
Department of Defense created the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response Office (SAPRO) back in 
2005. This was just one year after Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld established the Joint Task 
Force for Sexual Assault Prevention and Response as a single point of accountability for sexual assault 
policy within the DoD back in 2004.  

BWA Comments on Reproductive Health Services (RIN 2900-AS31) 
Page 2 of 3 
The U.S. DoD’s recently released FY 2024 SAPRO Report contains an Appendix B: Statistical Data on 
Sexual Assault. On page 9 of this appendix, an article in the American Journal of Preventative Medicine 
is referenced, noting that, “Research shows that reporting sexual assault increases the likelihood that 
victims will engage in medical treatment and other forms of assistance.” It also notes that “SAPRO 
encourages victims to report sexual assault, strives to improve response resources for victims, and 
supports victim participation in the military justice process, ‘as appropriate.’” 
On the next page, page 10 of the appendix, it notes that, “Sexual assault is an underreported crime 
among both the civilian and military populations, meaning that the number of individuals who report the 
crime to law enforcement falls far short of the number of individuals who have likely experienced the 
crime.” 
A 2024 study completed by the Costs of War Project at the Watson Institute of Brown University 
compared DoD data on sexual assaults with data that was not gathered from within the DoD to estimate 
sexual assault figures in the military since 2001. The study noted that “independent data suggest that 
actual sexual assault prevalence is two to four times higher than DoD estimations.” 
The National Sexual Violence Resource Center reports that rape is the most under-reported crime; 63% 
of sexual assaults are not reported to police, and only 12% of child sexual abuse is reported to the 
authorities. 
In the Annual Report on Sexual Harassment and Sexual Violence at the Military Service Academies for 
Academic Program Year 2023-2024, it notes on page 4 that still, over half (51%) of academy women 
experienced sexual harassment. On page 23, the report notes that the Family Advocacy Program (FAP) 
is the congressionally mandated program within DoD responsible for supplying clinical assessment, 
support, and treatment services in response to domestic abuse incidents. Sexual assault occurring within 
the context of a marriage or intimate partner relationship (sexual abuse) is a subset of domestic abuse.  
These facts and statistics stand as proof of the pervasiveness of sexual assault within the military and in 
the general community. In FY 2024, the Military Services received 8,195 reports of sexual assault 
involving service members as either victims or subjects. It is therefore disingenuous on the part of the 
VA to ignore this evidence in its proposal to reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion 
counseling from the VA medical benefits package. The fact that the VA is also proposing to reinstate the 
exclusions on abortion and abortion counseling for Civilian Health and Medical Program of the 
Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) is also egregious, especially since the VA stated in its 
proposed rule change that “We take this action to ensure that VA provides only needed medical services 
to our nation's heroes and their families.” 
Given the high rates of sexual assault within the U.S. Military Services (so high in fact that, again, DoD 
created a Sexual Assault Prevention and Reporting Office to address this crime and “improve response 
resources”), the Government of Guam contends that abortion and abortion counseling do in fact 
constitute a “needed medical service to our nation’s heroes and their families.” 
Another point to consider is that within Guam’s population of approximately 153,000, our island has 
much higher than the national average rates per capita of domestic violence and sexual assault crimes, 
according to the FBI Uniform Crime Report. With the influx of service members resulting from the

To abandon a veteran or a family member of a veteran who has been sexually assaulted - especially if a 
pregnancy results from that assault - and to tell that person that abortion services and abortion 
counseling are “not needed,” represents an astounding disconnect between those who have made the 
sacrifice to serve our country and those making the decisions within the U.S. Veterans Affairs Office 
and the U.S. Department of Defense.  
DoD has an admitted problem with sexual assault within its own ranks - over 8,000 reports in the last 
fiscal year alone. To admit this problem, but to tell veterans and their families that the VA will not pay 
for abortion services or abortion counseling is not acceptable.  It is also not, per the SAPRO, striving “to 
improve response resources for victims.” 
We strongly urge the VA NOT to reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from 
its medical benefits package. We urge the VA to cover all reproductive health options for service 
members, veterans, and their families. And to keep working to change the climate within the U.S. 
military that makes sexual assault so pervasive within its ranks. 
Si Yu’os Ma’ase for the opportunity to submit these comments on the VA proposed action to reinstate 
the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from its medical benefits package. 
Jayne T. Flores 
Director, Bureau of Women’s Affairs 
Government of Guam
